This word is often misused. Be careful. Players do *not* “comprise” a football team, and employees do *not* “comprise” a company. Nor can a football team be said to be “*comprised* of” players, or a company to be “*comprised* of” employees. These are common mistakes. Instead, you can say that players *constitute* or *compose* a team, and that employees *constitute* or *compose* a company.
You can also say that a team *consists* of players or a company *consists* of employees.

cards.pron: kun SIL ee uh tor ee
cards.definition: making peace; attempting to resolve a dispute through goodwill
cards.example:
Come on—be *conciliatory!*
The formerly warring countries were *conciliatory* at the treaty conference.
After dinner at the all-you-can-eat pancake house, the divorced couple began to feel *conciliatory*, so they flew to Las Vegas and were remarried.
The accountant managed to *reconcile* the company books with the cash on hand only with great creativity.
cards.notes:
To be *conciliatory* is to kiss and make up.
When peace has been made, we say that the warring parties have come to a *reconciliation* (rek un sil ee AY shun). To *reconcile* (REK un syle) is to bring two things into agreement.

cards.definition: brief and to the point; succinct
cards.example: The scientist’s explanation was *concise;* it was brief and it helped us understand the difficult concept.
cards.notes: To be *concise* is to say much with few words. A *concise* speaker is one who speaks *concisely* or with *concision*.

cards.definition: harmony; agreement
cards.example:
The war between the neighboring tribes ended thirty years of *concord*.
The faculty meeting was marked by *concord;* no one yelled at anyone else.
cards.notes:
Nations that live in *concord* are nations that live together in peace.
*Discord* is the opposite of *concord*. A faculty meeting where everyone yelled at one another would be a faculty meeting marked by *discord*. It would be a *discordant* meeting.
An *accord* is a formal agreement, usually reached after a dispute.

cards.definition: happening at the same time; parallel
cards.example:
The criminal was sentenced to two *concurrent* fifteen-year sentences; the sentences will run at the same time, and he will be out of jail in fifteen years.
High prices, falling demand, and poor weather were three *concurrent* trends that made life especially difficult for corn farmers last month.
The assistant wanted to keep his job, so he always *concurred* with his boss.

cards.definition: to stoop to someone else’s level, usually in an offensive way; to patronize
cards.example: I was surprised that the president of the company had *condescended* to talk with me, a mere temporary employee.
cards.notes:
= stoop or patronize
Many grown-ups make the mistake of *condescending* to young children, who usually prefer to be treated as equals, or at least as rational beings.

cards.definition: to overlook; to permit to happen
cards.example: The principal *condoned* the hoods’ smoking in the bathroom; he simply ignored it.
cards.notes: To *condone* what someone does is to look the other way while it happens or to permit it to happen by not doing anything about it.

cards.definition: promoting
cards.example:
The chairs in the library are *conducive* to sleep. If you sit in them to study, you will fall asleep.
The foul weather was not *conducive* to our having a picnic.

cards.definition: a flowing together, especially of rivers; the place where they begin to flow together
cards.example:
The *confluence* of the Missouri and Mississippi rivers is at St. Louis; that’s the place where they join together.
There is a remarkable *confluence* in our thoughts: We think the same way about almost everything.
A *confluence* of many factors (no ice, bad food, terrible music) made it inevitable that the party would be a flop.

cards.definition: agreeably suitable; pleasant
cards.example:
The little cabin in the woods was *congenial* to the writer; he was able to get a lot of writing done there.
The new restaurant has a *congenial* atmosphere. We enjoy just sitting there playing with the ice in our water glasses.
cards.notes:
When people get along together at a restaurant and don’t throw food at one another, they are being *congenial*.
*Genial* and *congenial* share similar meanings. *Genial* means pleasing, kind, sympathetic, or helpful. You can be pleased by a *genial* manner or by a *genial* climate.

cards.definition: describing a trait or condition acquired between conception and birth; innate
cards.notes:
A *congenital* birth defect is one that is present at birth but was not caused by one’s genes.
The word is also used more loosely to describe any (usually bad) trait or behavior that is so firmly fixed it seems to be a part of a person’s nature.
A *congenital* liar is a natural liar, a person who can’t help but lie.

cards.definition: to come together
cards.example:
Protestors were granted permission to *congregate* peacefully on the plaza.
About half the *congregation* attended the sunrise service.
cards.notes:
= get together
The noun form is *congregation* and can refer to the membership of a house of worship.
*Aggregate* also has to do with coming together. Can you think of additional words with the same root?

cards.definition: to guess; to deduce or infer on slight evidence
cards.example:
If forced to *conjecture*, I would say the volcano will erupt in twenty-four hours.
The divorce lawyer for Mr. Davis argued that the putative cause of the lipstick on his collar was mere *conjecture*.
cards.notes:
*Conjecture* can also be a noun.
A *conjecture* is *conjectural*.

cards.definition: to summon or bring into being as if by magic
cards.example:
The chef *conjured* (or *conjured* up) a fabulous gourmet meal using nothing more than the meager ingredients in Lucy’s kitchen.
The wizard *conjured* (or *conjured* up) an evil spirit by mumbling some magic words and throwing a little powdered eye of newt into the fire.

cards.definition: an expert, particularly in matters of art or taste
cards.example:
The artist’s work was popular, but *connoisseurs* rejected it as amateurish.
Frank was a *connoisseur* of bad movies. He had seen them all and knew which ones were genuinely dreadful and which ones were merely poorly made.
The meal was exquisite enough to impress a *connoisseur*.
I like sculpture, but I’m no *connoisseur;* I probably can’t describe to you why one statue is better than another.

cards.definition: to make or declare sacred
cards.example:
The Veterans Day speaker said that the battlefield had been *consecrated* by the blood of the soldiers who had died there.
The priest *consecrated* the building by sprinkling holy water on it.
The college chaplain delivered a sermon at the *consecration* (kahn suh KRAY shun) ceremony for the new chapel.
Their act of vandalism was a *desecration*.
Doodling in a book *desecrates* the book, even if the book isn’t a Bible.
The graffiti on the front door of the school is a *desecration*.
cards.notes:
= make sacred
The opposite of *consecrate* is *desecrate* (DES uh krayt), which means to treat irreverently. The vandals *desecrated* the cemetery by knocking down all the tombstones.
*Desecrate* can also be applied to areas outside religion.

cards.definition: unanimity or general agreement
cards.notes:
When there is a *consensus*, everybody feels the same way.
Contrary to how the word is often used, *consensus* implies more than just a rough agreement or a majority opinion. Election results don’t reflect a *consensus* unless everyone or nearly everyone votes for the same candidate.

cards.definition: harmonious; in agreement
cards.example:
Our desires were *consonant* with theirs; we all wanted the same thing.
The decision to construct a new gymnasium was *consonant* with the superintendent’s belief in physical education.
cards.notes: The opposite of *consonant* is *dissonant* (DIS uh nunt), which means inharmonious. *Dissonant* voices are voices that don’t sound good together.

cards.definition: to interpret
cards.example:
Preston *construed* his contract as giving him the right to do anything he wanted.
The law had always been *construed* as permitting the behavior for which Katya had been arrested.
The meaning of the poem, as I *construed* it, had to do with the love of a man for his dog.
Tommy *misconstrued* Pamela’s smile, but he certainly did not *misconstrue* the slap she gave him.

cards.definition: perfect; complete; supremely skillful
cards.example: A *consummate* pianist is an extremely good one. Nothing is lacking in the way he or she plays.
cards.notes: *Consummate* (KAHN suh mayt) is also a verb. Notice the different pronunciation. To *consummate* something is to finish it or make it complete. Signing a contract would *consummate* an agreement.

cards.definition: argumentative; quarrelsome
cards.example: Liz figured that her *contentious* style would make her a perfect litigator; after law school, however, the would-be trial attorney discovered that passing the bar requires more than a will to argue.
cards.notes:
A person looking for a fight is *contentious*.
Two people having a fight are *contentious*.
To be *contentious* in a discussion is to make a lot of noisy objections.
A *contender* is a fighter. To *contend* is to fight or argue for something. Someone who breaks the law may have to *contend* with the law.

cards.definition: side by side; adjoining
cards.notes:
Two countries that share a border are *contiguous;* so are two events that happened one right after the other.
If two countries are *contiguous*, the territory they cover is continuous. That is, it spreads or continues across both countries without any interruption.

cards.definition: dependent; possible
cards.example:
Our agreement to buy their house is *contingent* upon the sellers’ finding another house to move into. That is, they won’t sell their house to us unless they can find another house to buy.
My happiness is *contingent* on yours; if you’re unhappy, I’m unhappy.
The Bowdens were prepared for any *contingency*. Their front hall closet contained a first-aid kit, a fire extinguisher, a life raft, a parachute, and a pack of sled dogs.
Several *contingencies* stand between us and the successful completion of our business proposal; several things could happen to screw it up.
cards.notes: A *contingency* is a possibility or something that may happen but is at least as likely not to happen.

cards.definition: admitting guilt; especially feeling remorseful
cards.example: Mira was *contrite* about her mistake, so we forgave her.
cards.notes:
To be *contrite* is to admit whatever terrible thing you did.
A criminal who won’t confess his crime is not *contrite*.
Saying that you’re sorry is an act of *contrition* (kun TRISH un).

cards.definition: artificial; labored
cards.example:
Sam’s acting was *contrived:* No one in the audience believed his character or enjoyed his performance.
The artist was widely admired for his originality, but his paintings seemed *contrived* to me.
No one laughed at Mark’s *contrived* attempt at humor.
cards.notes: A *contrivance* is a mechanical device, usually something rigged up.

cards.definition: common; customary; unexceptional
cards.example:
The architect’s *conventional* designs didn’t win him awards for originality.
The bland politician maintained his popularity by never straying far from the *conventional* wisdom about any topic.
cards.notes:
Tipping the waiter in a restaurant is a *conventional* courtesy.
*Conventional* wisdom is what everyone thinks.

cards.definition: fond of partying; festive
cards.notes:
A *convivial* gathering is one in which the people present enjoy eating, drinking, and being together.
To be *convivial* is to be an eager but generally well-behaved party animal.
A *convivial* person is the opposite of an antisocial person.

cards.definition: abundant; plentiful
cards.example:
The champagne at the wedding reception was *copious* but not very good.
Matt had a *copious* supply of nails in his workshop. Everywhere you stepped, it seemed, there was a pile of nails.
Phil ate *copiously* at the banquet and went home feeling quite sick.

cards.definition: something that follows; a natural consequence
cards.example:
Bloodshed and death are *corollaries* of any declaration of war.
Higher prices were a *corollary* of the two companies’ agreement not to compete.
cards.notes: In mathematics, a *corollary* is a law that can be deduced without further proof from a law that has already been proven.

cards.definition: to confirm; to back up with evidence
cards.example:
I knew my statement was correct when my colleague *corroborated* it.
Henny Penny’s contention that the sky was falling could not be *corroborated*. That is, no one was able to find any fallen sky.
The police could find no evidence of theft and thus could not *corroborate* Greg’s claim that he had been robbed.

cards.definition: at home in many places or situations; internationally sophisticated
cards.example:
Marcello’s interests were *cosmopolitan*—he liked Greek wine, German beer, Dutch cheese, Japanese cars, and French fries.
A truly *cosmopolitan* traveler never feels like a foreigner anywhere on Earth.
New York is a *cosmopolitan* city; you can hear nearly every language spoken there.

cards.definition: face; facial expression, especially an encouraging one
cards.example:
His father’s confident *countenance* gave Lou the courage to persevere.
Ed’s harsh words belied his *countenance*, which was kind and encouraging.
Dad *countenanced* our backyard rock fights even though he didn’t really approve of them.
cards.notes: *Countenance* can also be a verb. To *countenance* something is to condone it or tolerate it.

cards.definition: a brilliant victory or accomplishment; the violent overthrow of a government by a small internal group
cards.example:
Winning a gold medal at the Olympics was a real *coup* for the fifty-year-old man.
The student council’s great *coup* was persuading Foo Fighters to play at our prom.
In the attempted *coup* in the Philippines, some army officers tried to take over the government.
cards.notes: The full name for this type of *coup* is *coup d’état* (koo day TAH). A *coup de grace* (koo duh GRAHS) is a final blow or concluding event.

cards.definition: a solemn agreement; a contract; a pledge
cards.example:
The warring tribes made a *covenant* not to fight each other anymore.
We signed a *covenant* never to drive Masha’s father’s car without permission again.

cards.definition: secret; hidden
cards.notes:
To be *covert* is to be covered.
*Covert* activities are secret activities.
A *covert* military operation is one the public knows nothing about.
The opposite of *covert* is *overt. Overt* (OH vurt) means open or unconcealed.

cards.definition: to wish for enviously
cards.example:
To *covet* thy neighbor’s wife is to want thy neighbor’s wife for thyself.
Any position at MTV is a highly *coveted* job.
cards.notes: To be *covetous* is to be envious.

cards.definition: eager to believe; gullible
cards.example:
The *credulous* housewife believed that she had won a million dollars through an email scam.
Judy was so *credulous* that she simply nodded happily when Kirven told her he could teach her how to fly. Judy’s *credulity* (kri DYOOL uh tee) was limitless.
Larry’s implausible story of heroism was not *credible*. Still, *credulous* old Louis believed it.
No one could prove Frank’s theory, but his standing at the university helped it gain *credence*.
Our record in raising money was very *creditable;* we raised several thousand dollars every year.
cards.notes:
*Credulous* should not be confused with *credible*. To be *credible* is to be believable. Almost anything, however *incredible*, is *credible* to a *credulous* person.
A story that cannot be believed is *incredible*. If you don’t believe that story someone just told you, you are *incredulous*. If something is *credible*, it may gain *credence* (KREED uns), which means belief or intellectual acceptance.
Another similar word is *creditable*, which means worthy of credit or praise.

cards.definition: standard; basis for judgment
cards.example:
When Norm judges a meal, he has only one *criterion:* Is it edible?
In choosing among the linemen, the most important *criterion* was quickness.
cards.notes: The plural of *criterion* is *criteria*. You can’t have *one criteria;* you can only have one *criterion*. If you have two or more, you have *criteria*. There is no such thing as *criterions* and no such thing as *a criteria*.

cards.definition: mysterious; mystifying
cards.example:
Elaine’s remarks were *cryptic;* Jerry was baffled by what she said.
The ghost made *cryptic* comments about the *crypt* from which he had just emerged; that is, no one could figure out what the ghost meant.
cards.notes: A *cryptic* statement is one in which something important remains hidden.

cards.definition: relating to cooking or the kitchen
cards.example: Allison pursued her *culinary* interests by attending the *culinary* institute. Her first meal, which was burned beyond recognition, was a *culinary* disaster.
cards.notes:
= related to cooking
A cooking school is sometimes called a *culinary* institute.

cards.definition: to climax; to reach full effect
cards.example:
Connie’s years of practice *culminated* in a great victory at the international juggling championship.
The masquerade ball was the *culmination* of our fund-raising efforts.

cards.definition: deserving blame; guilty
cards.example:
The accountant’s failure to spot the errors made him *culpable* in the tax-fraud case.
We all felt *culpable* when the homeless old man died in the doorway of our apartment building.
Lou’s confession didn’t *exculpate* Bob, because one of the things that Lou confessed was that Bob had helped him do it.
cards.notes:
A person who is *culpable* (a *culprit*) is one who can be blamed for doing something.
To decide that a person is not *culpable* after all is to *exculpate* (EK skul payt) that person.
The opposite of *exculpate* is *inculpate*. To *inculpate* is to accuse someone of something.

cards.definition: hasty; superficial
cards.example:
To give a book a *cursory* reading is to skim it quickly without comprehending much.
The *cursor* on Dave’s computer made a *cursory* sweep across the data as he scrolled down the page.
cards.notes: To make a *cursory* attempt at learning French is to memorize a couple of easy words and then give up.

cards.definition: to shorten; to cut short
cards.example: The vet *curtailed* his effort to cut the cat’s tail with the lawn mower. That is, he stopped trying.
cards.notes: To *curtail* a tale is to cut it short.

cards.definition: one who deeply distrusts human nature; one who believes humans are motivated only by selfishness
cards.example: When the pop star gave a million dollars to the museum, *cynics* said he was merely trying to buy himself a reputation as a cultured person.
cards.notes:
= one who distrusts humanity
To be *cynical* is to be extremely suspicious of the motivations of other people.
*Cynicism* is general grumpiness and pessimism about human nature.

cards.definition: to make fearful; to intimidate
cards.example:
The steepness of the mountain *daunted* the team of amateur climbers, because they hadn’t realized what they were in for.
The size of the players on the visiting team was *daunting;* the players on the home team began to perspire nervously.
The rescue crew was *undaunted* by the flames and ran into the burning house to look for survivors. The entire crew was *dauntless* in its effort to save the people inside.
cards.notes: To be *dauntless* or *undaunted* is to be fearless or unintimidated.

cards.definition: lack; scarcity
cards.example:
There is no *dearth* of comedy at a convention of clowns.
When there is a *dearth* of food, many people may starve.
There was a *dearth* of gaiety at the boring Christmas party.

cards.definition: violent breakdown; sudden overthrow; overwhelming defeat
cards.example: A political debate would become a *debacle* if the candidates began screaming and throwing dinner rolls at each other.
cards.notes: This word can also be pronounced “day BAHK ul.”

cards.definition: wild living; excessive intemperance
cards.example: *Debauchery* can be expensive; fortunately for Jeff, his wallet matched his appetite for extravagant pleasures. He died a poor, albeit happy, man.
cards.notes: To *debauch* is to seduce or corrupt. Someone who is *debauched* has been seduced or corrupted.

cards.definition: to weaken; to cripple
cards.example:
The football player’s career was ended by a *debilitating* injury to his knee.
A surgeon who becomes *debilitated* is one who has lost the ability to operate on the *debilities* of other people.
cards.notes: To become *debilitated* is to suffer a *debility*, which is the opposite of an ability.

cards.definition: decaying or decayed, especially in terms of morals
cards.example: Carousing in local bars instead of going to class is *decadent*.
cards.notes:
A person who engages in *decadent* behavior is a person whose morals have decayed or fallen into ruin.
*Decadent* behavior is often an affectation of bored young people. The noun is *decadence*.

cards.definition: to kill or destroy a large part of
cards.example:
When locusts attack a crop, they sometimes *decimate* it, leaving very little that’s fit for human consumption.
You might say in jest that your family had *decimated* its turkey dinner on Thanksgiving, leaving nothing but a few crumbs and a pile of bones.
cards.notes:
= kill a large part of
To *decimate* an army is to come close to wiping it out.
The noun is *decimation*.

cards.definition: proper; in good taste; orderly
cards.example: The New Year’s Eve crowd was relatively *decorous* until midnight, when they went wild.
cards.notes:
*Decorous* behavior is good, polite, orderly behavior. To be *decorous* is to be sober and tasteful.
To behave *decorously* is to behave with *decorum* (di KOR um).

cards.definition: to conclude from the evidence; to infer
cards.example:
From the footprints on the ground, Clarice *deduced* that the criminal had feet.
Daffy *deduced* from the shape of its bill that the duck was really a chicken. That the duck was really a chicken was Daffy’s *deduction*.
cards.notes:
= conclude from evidence
To *deduce* something is to conclude it without being told it directly.

cards.definition: to libel or slander; to ruin the good name of
cards.example:
The local businessman accused the newspaper of *defaming* him by publishing an article that said his company was poorly managed.
The businessman who believed he had been *defamed* by the newspaper sued the paper’s publisher for *defamation*.
cards.notes:
To *defame* someone is to make accusations that harm the person’s reputation.
To *defame* is to take away fame, to take away a good name.
To suffer such a loss of reputation is to suffer *defamation*.

cards.definition: submission to another’s will; respect; courtesy
cards.example:
Dean showed *deference* to his grandfather: He let the old man have first dibs on the birthday cake.
Danny stopped texting at the dinner table in *deference* to the wishes of his mother.
Joe was supposed to go first, but he *deferred* to Steve, who had been waiting longer.
Joe was being *deferential* when he allowed Steve to go first.
cards.notes:
To show *deference* to another is to place that person’s wishes ahead of your own.
To show *deference* to another is to *defer* to that person.
To show *deference* is also to be *deferential* (def uh REN shul).

cards.definition: conclusive; providing the last word
cards.example:
Walter wrote the *definitive* biography of Keats; nothing more could have been added by another book.
The army completely wiped out the invaders; its victory was *definitive*.
No one could find anything to object to in Cindy’s *definitive* explanation of how the meteorite had gotten into the bathtub.

cards.definition: to break down; to deteriorate
cards.example:
The discussion quickly *degenerated* into an argument.
Over the years, the nice old neighborhood had *degenerated* into a terrible slum.
The fans’ behavior *degenerated* as the game went on.
The mood of the party was spoiled when a drunken *degenerate* wandered in from off the street.
The slum neighborhood was *degenerate*.
The fans’ *degenerate* behavior prompted the police to make several arrests.
cards.notes:
A person whose behavior has *degenerated* can be referred to as a *degenerate* (di JEN ur it).
*Degenerate* (di JEN ur it) can also be an adjective, meaning *degenerated*.

cards.definition: harmful
cards.example:
Smoking cigarettes is *deleterious* to your health.
Is watching a lot of TV really *deleterious?* Of course not.

cards.definition: to describe accurately; to draw in outline
cards.example:
After Jack had *delineated* his plan, we had no doubt about what he intended to do.
Sharon’s peculiar feelings about her pet gorilla were *delineated* in the newspaper article about her.
The portrait artist *delineated* Sarah’s features then filled in the shading.

cards.definition: to deceive
cards.example:
The con man *deluded* us into thinking that he would make us rich. Instead, he tricked us into giving him several hundred dollars.
The *deluded* mental patient believed that he was a chicken sandwich.
Lori is so persuasive that she was able to *delude* Leslie into thinking she was a countess.
That he was a great poet was the *delusion* of the English teacher, who could scarcely write two complete sentences in a row.
Todd, the well-known jerk, suffered from the *delusion* that he was a genuinely nice man.
cards.notes: To be *deluded* is to suffer from a *delusion*.

cards.definition: a flood; an inundation
cards.example: The $1 million reward for the lost poodle brought in a *deluge* of hot leads. The distraught owner was *deluged* by phone calls all week.
cards.notes: A *deluge* is a flood, but the word is often used figuratively.

cards.definition: a leader who uses prejudice to get more power
cards.notes:
= rabble-rousing leader
A *demagogue* is a leader, but not in a good sense of the word. He manipulates the public to support his aims, but he is little different from a dictator. A *demagogue* is often a despot.
This word can also be spelled *demagog*. The methods a *demagogue* uses are *demagoguery* (DEM uh gahg uh ree) or *demagogy* (DEM uh gahg ee).

cards.definition: inhabitant
cards.notes:
To be a *denizen* of a country is to live there. A citizen of a country is usually also a *denizen*.
To be a *denizen* of a restaurant is to go there often—so often that people begin to wonder whether you live there.
Fish are sometimes referred to as “*denizens* of the deep.” Don’t refer to them this way yourself; the expression is a cliché.

cards.definition: extreme wickedness or corruption
cards.example: Mrs. Prudinkle wondered whether the *depravity* of her class of eight-year-olds was the result of their watching Saturday morning television.
cards.notes: To exhibit *depravity* is to be *depraved* (di PRAYVD).

cards.definition: to express disapproval of
cards.example:
To *deprecate* a colleague’s work is to risk making yourself unwelcome in your colleague’s office.
The critic’s *deprecating* comments about my new novel put me in a bad mood for an entire month.
To be *self-deprecating* is to belittle one’s own efforts, often in the hope that someone else will say, “No, you’re wonderful!”
cards.notes:
“This stinks!” is a *deprecating* remark.
A very similar word is *depreciate* (dih PREE shee ayt). To *depreciate* a colleague’s work would be to represent it as being of little value. For another meaning of *depreciate*, see *appreciate*.

cards.definition: to ridicule; to laugh at contemptuously
cards.example:
Gerald *derided* Diana’s driving ability after their hair-raising trip down the twisting mountain road.
Sportswriters *derided* Columbia’s football team, which hadn’t won a game in three years.
The boss *derided* his secretary mercilessly, so she quit her job. She was someone who could not accept *derision* (di RIZH un).

cards.definition: disapproving; degrading
cards.example: Stephen could never seem to think of anything nice to say about anyone; virtually all of his comments were *derogatory*.
cards.notes: *Derogatory* remarks are negative remarks expressing disapproval. They are nastier than merely critical remarks.

cards.definition: to dry out
cards.example:
The hot wind *desiccated* the few grapes remaining on the vine; after a day or two, they looked like raisins.
After a week without water, the *desiccated* plant fell over and died.
cards.notes: Plums become prunes through a process of *desiccation*.

cards.definition: extremely depressed; full of despair
cards.example:
The cook became *despondent* when the wedding cake fell on the floor fifteen minutes before the reception.
After the death of his wife, the man was *despondent* for many months.
The team fell into *despondency* after losing the state championship game by a single point.

cards.definition: an absolute ruler; an autocrat
cards.example:
Stephen was a *despot;* workers who disagreed with him were fired.
The island kingdom was ruled by a ruthless *despot* who executed suspected rebels at noon each day in the village square.
There was cheering in the street when the country’s *despotic* government was overthrown.
cards.notes: To act like a *despot* is to be *despotic* (di SPAH tik).

cards.definition: extremely poor; utterly lacking
cards.notes:
*Destitute* people are people without money or possessions, or with very little money and very few possessions.
To be left *destitute* is to be left without money or property. The word can also be used figuratively. A teacher might accuse her students of being *destitute* of brains, or intellectually *destitute*.

cards.definition: without a plan or purpose; disconnected; random
cards.example:
Aadi made a few *desultory* attempts to start a garden, but nothing came of them.
In his *desultory* address, Rizal skipped from one topic to another and never came to the point.
The discussion at our meeting was *desultory;* no one’s comments seemed to bear any relation to anyone else’s.

cards.definition: skillful; adroit
cards.example:
Though not imposing in stature, Rashid was the most *dextrous* basketball player on the court; he often beat taller competitors with his nimble management of the ball.
Ilya was determined not to sell the restaurant on eBay; even the most *dextrous* negotiator could not sway him.
cards.notes:
*Dextrous* often, but not always, connotes physical ability. Like *adroit*, it comes from the Latin word for right (as in the direction), because right-handed people were once considered physically and mentally superior.
You may also see this word spelled *dexterous. Dexterity* is the noun form. For an antonym, see *gauche*.

cards.definition: relating to discussions; relating to the rules and methods of reasoning; approaching truth in the middle of opposing extremes
cards.notes:
The game of Twenty Questions is *dialectical*, in that the participants attempt to narrow down a chosen object by asking a series of ever more specific questions.
The noun is *dialectic*.

cards.definition: an authoritative saying; an adage; a maxim; a proverb
cards.notes: “No pain, no gain” is a hackneyed *dictum* of sadistic coaches everywhere.

cards.definition: intended to teach; morally instructive; pedantic
cards.example:
Luther’s seemingly amusing talk had a *didactic* purpose; he was trying to show his listeners the difference between right and wrong.
The priest’s conversation was always *didactic*. He never said anything that wasn’t intended to teach a lesson.
The new novel is painfully *didactic;* the author’s aim is always to instruct and never to entertain.

cards.definition: timid; lacking in self-confidence
cards.example:
The *diffident* student never made a single comment in class.
Sebastian’s stammer made him *diffident* in conversation and shy in groups of strangers.
Carla’s *diffidence* led many participants to believe she hadn’t been present at the meeting, even though she had.

cards.definition: to stray from the main subject
cards.example: After a lengthy *digression*, the lecturer returned to his speech and brought it to a conclusion.
cards.notes:
Speaking metaphorically, to *digress* is to leave the main highway in order to travel aimlessly on back roads. When a speaker *digresses*, he departs from the main topic and tells a story only distantly related to it.
Such a story is called a *digression*. Sometimes a writer’s or speaker’s *digressions* are more interesting than his or her main points.

cards.definition: someone with superficial knowledge of the arts; an amateur; a dabbler
cards.example:
Reginald said he was an artist, but he was merely a *dilettante;* he didn’t know a pencil from a paintbrush.
Antonella dismissed the members of the ladies’ sculpture club as nothing more than a bunch of *dilettantes*.
cards.notes: To be a *dilettante* is to dabble in something rather than doing it in a serious way.

cards.definition: to have insight; to see things clearly; to discriminate; to differentiate
cards.example: The ill-mannered people at Tisha’s party proved that she had little *discernment* when it came to choosing friends.
cards.notes: To *discern* something is to perceive it clearly. A writer whose work demonstrates *discernment* is a writer who is a keen observer.

cards.definition: prudent; judiciously reserved
cards.example:
The psychiatrist was very *discreet;* no matter how much we pestered him, he wouldn’t gossip about the problems of his famous patients.
It was *indiscreet* of Laura to tell Salima how much she hated Bailey’s new hairstyle, because Salima always tells Bailey everything.
When Laura told Salima, she committed an *indiscretion*.
cards.notes:
To make *discreet* inquiries is to ask around without letting the whole world know you’re doing it.
He had *discretion* (di SKRESH un).
To be *indiscreet* is to be imprudent and especially to say or do things you shouldn’t.

cards.definition: unconnected; separate; distinct
cards.example:
The twins were identical but their personalities were *discrete*.
The drop in the stock market was not the result of any single force but of many *discrete* trends.
cards.notes:
Do not confuse *discrete* with *discreet*.
When things are all jumbled up together, they are said to be *indiscrete*, which means not separated or sorted.

cards.definition: to notice or point out the difference between two or more things; to discern; to differentiate
cards.notes: *Indiscriminate* means not *discriminating;* in other words, random or haphazard.

cards.definition: arrogant scorn; contempt
cards.example:
Bertram viewed the hot dog with *disdain*, believing that to eat such a disgusting food was beneath him.
The millionaire looked upon the poor workers with evident *disdain*.
cards.notes:
*Disdain* can also be a verb. The millionaire in the previous example could be said to have *disdained* those workers.
To be filled with *disdain* is to be *disdainful*.

cards.definition: not taking sides; unbiased
cards.example:
A referee should be *disinterested*. He or she should not be rooting for one of the competing teams.
Meredith claimed that the accident had been Louie’s fault, but several *disinterested* witnesses said that Meredith had actually bashed into his car after jumping the median and driving in the wrong lane for several miles.
cards.notes:
*Disinterested* should *not* be used to mean *uninterested*. If you don’t care about knowing something, you are *uninterested*, not *disinterested*.
A *disinterested* observer is one who has no personal stake in or attachment to what is being observed.

cards.definition: to belittle; to say uncomplimentary things about, usually in a somewhat indirect way
cards.example:
The mayor *disparaged* our efforts to beautify the town square when he said that the flower bed we had planted looked somewhat worse than the bed of weeds it had replaced.
My guidance counselor *disparaged* my high school record by telling me that not everybody belongs in college.

cards.definition: different; incompatible; unequal
cards.example:
Our interests were *disparate:* Cathy liked to play with dolls, and I liked to throw her dolls out the window.
The *disparate* interest groups were united only by their intense dislike of the candidate.
The novel was difficult to read because the plot consisted of dozens of *disparate* threads that never came together.
cards.notes: The noun form of *disparate* is *disparity* (dih SPAR i tee). *Disparity* means inequality. The opposite of *disparity* is *parity*.

cards.definition: to spread the seeds of something; to scatter; to make widely known
cards.notes:
= spread seeds
News is *disseminated* through many media: internet, radio, television, newspapers, magazines, and gossips.

cards.definition: to thin out, drift away, or dissolve; to cause to thin out, drift away, or dissolve; to waste or squander
cards.example:
The smoke *dissipated* as soon as we opened the windows.
llya’s anger *dissipated* as the day wore on, and he gradually forgot what had upset him.
The police *dissipated* the riotous crowd by spraying the demonstrators with fire hoses and firing rubber bullets over their heads.
Alex won the weekly lottery but *dissipated* the entire winnings in one abandoned, fun-filled weekend.
cards.notes: We can also say that a person is *dissipated*, by which we mean that he indulges in wild living. Alex is *dissipated*.

cards.definition: the breaking up or dissolving of something into parts; disintegration
cards.example: Nothing could prevent the *dissolution* of the Jesse Ventura Fan Club after he retired to seek a political career.
cards.notes: A person who is *dissolute* has lived life in the fast lane too long. *Dissolute* and *dissipated* are synonyms in this sense.

cards.definition: to swell; to extend a great deal
cards.example:
The tire *distended* alarmingly as the forgetful gas station attendant kept pumping more and more air into it.
A *distended* belly is one symptom of malnutrition.

cards.definition: to tell apart; to cause to stand out
cards.example:
The rodent expert’s eyesight was so acute that he was able to *distinguish* between a shrew and a vole at more than a thousand paces.
I studied and studied but I was never able to *distinguish* between *discrete* and *discreet*.
His face had no *distinguishing* characteristics; there was nothing about his features that stuck in your memory.
Lou’s uneventful career as a dogcatcher was not *distinguished* by adventure or excitement.

cards.definition: easily taught; obedient; easy to handle
cards.example:
The *docile* students quietly memorized all the lessons their teacher told them.
The baby raccoons appeared *docile* at first, but they were almost impossible to control.
Mia’s *docility* (dah SIL i tee) fooled the professor into believing that she was incapable of thinking for herself.

cards.definition: inflexibly committed to a doctrine or theory without regard to its practicality; dogmatic
cards.notes:
= committed to a theory
A *doctrinaire* supporter of manned space flights to Pluto would be someone who supported such space flights even though it might be shown that such lengthy journeys could never be undertaken.
A *doctrinaire* opponent of fluoridation of water would be someone whose opposition could not be shaken by proof that fluoride is good for teeth and not bad for anything else.
A person with *doctrinaire* views can be called a *doctrinaire*.

cards.definition: arrogantly assertive of unproven ideas; stubbornly claiming that something (often a system of beliefs) is beyond dispute
cards.example:
Marty is *dogmatic* on the subject of the creation of the world; he sneers at anyone whose views are not identical to his.
The philosophy professor became increasingly *dogmatic* as he grew older and became more firmly convinced of his strange theories.
cards.notes:
A *dogma* is a belief. A *dogmatic* person, however, is stubbornly convinced of his beliefs.
The opinions or ideas *dogmatically* asserted by a *dogmatic* person are known collectively as *dogma*.

cards.definition: having to do with the household or family; not foreign
cards.notes:
= of the household
A home that enjoys *domestic* tranquillity is a happy home.
A maid is sometimes referred to as a *domestic* engineer or simply as a *domestic*.
To be *domestic* is to enjoy being at home or to be skillful at doing things around the house.
*Domestic* wine is wine from this country, as opposed to wine imported from, say, France.
The *domestic* steel industry is the steel industry in this country.
A country that enjoys *domestic* tranquillity is a happy country on the homefront.

cards.definition: inactive; as though asleep; asleep
cards.example:
Mt. Vesuvius erupted violently and then fell *dormant* for several hundred years.
Frank’s interest in playing the piano was *dormant* and, quite possibly, dead.
The snow fell silently over the *dormant* village, which became snarled in traffic jams the following morning.
cards.notes:
*Dormant*, like *dormitory*, comes from a root meaning sleep.
Many plants remain *dormant* through the winter; that is, they stop growing until spring.
The noun is *dormancy*.

cards.definition: j full of doubt; uncertain
cards.example:
I was fairly certain that I would be able to fly if I could merely flap my arms hard enough, but Mary was *dubious;* she said I’d better flap my legs as well.
We were *dubious* about the team’s chance of success and, as it turned out, our *dubiety* (doo BYE uh tee) was justified: The team lost.
Sam’s chances of getting the job were *doubtful* because the employer was *dubious* of his claim that he had been president of the United States while in high school.
cards.notes:
*Dubious* and *doubtful* don’t mean exactly the same thing. A *dubious* person is a person who has doubts. A *doubtful* outcome is an outcome that isn’t certain to occur.
Something beyond doubt is *indubitable*. A dogmatic person believes his opinions are *indubitable*.

cards.definition: the act of being two-faced; double-dealing; deception
cards.example:
Dave, in his *duplicity*, told us he wasn’t going to rob the bank and then went right out and robbed it.
Liars engage in *duplicity* all the time; they say one thing and do another.
The *duplicitous* salesman sold the red sports car to someone else even though he had promised to sell it to us.

cards.definition: boiling; bubbling with excitement; exuberant
cards.example: Cammie was *ebullient* when her fairy godmother said she could use one of her three wishes to wish for three more wishes.
cards.notes:
A boiling liquid can be called *ebullient*. More often, though, this word describes excited or enthusiastic people.
The roaring crowd in a full stadium before the World Series might be said to be *ebullient*.
A person overflowing with enthusiasm might be said to be *ebullient*.
Someone or something that is *ebullient* is characterized by *ebullience*

cards.definition: not conventional; a little kooky; irregular
cards.example:
The *eccentric* inventor spent all his waking hours fiddling with what he said was a time machine, but it was actually just an old telephone booth.
Fred’s political views are *eccentric:* He believes that we should have kings instead of presidents and that the government should raise money by holding bake sales.
The rocket followed an *eccentric* course; first it veered in one direction, then it veered in another, then it crashed.
cards.notes: An *eccentric* person is a person who has *eccentricities* (ek sen TRIS uh teez).

cards.definition: choosing the best from many sources; drawn from many sources
cards.example:
Adolfo’s taste in art was *eclectic*. He liked the Old Masters, the Impressionists, and Walt Disney.
The *eclectic* menu included dishes from many different countries.
George’s *eclectic* reading made him well rounded.

cards.definition: to enlighten; to instruct, especially in moral or religious matters
cards.example:
We found the pastor’s sermon on the importance of not eating beans to be most *edifying*.
The teacher’s goal was to *edify* her students, not to force a handful of facts down their throats.
We would have felt lost at the art show had not the excellent and informative programs been provided for our *edification*.

cards.definition: to erase; to rub away the features of
cards.example:
The inscription on the tombstone had been *effaced* by centuries of weather.
The vandals *effaced* the delicate carving by rubbing it with sandpaper.
We tried to *efface* the dirty words that had been written on the front of our house, but nothing would remove them.
John is *self-effacing:* When he won an Olympic gold medal, all he said was, “Aw, shucks. I’m just a regular fella.”
cards.notes: To be *self-effacing* is to be modest.

cards.definition: a pouring forth
cards.example:
When the child was rescued from the well, there was an intense *effusion* of emotion from the crowd that had gathered around the hole.
The madman’s writings consisted of a steady *effusion* of nonsense.
Anna’s *effusive* thanks for our silly little present made us feel somewhat embarrassed, so we decided to move to a different lunch table.
cards.notes: To be *effusive* is to be highly emotional.

cards.pron: ih gal uh TAYR ee un
cards.definition: believing in the social and economic equality of all people
cards.example: People often lose interest in *egalitarian* measures when such measures interfere with their own interests.
cards.notes:
= believing in social equality
*Egalitarian* can also be used as a noun to characterize a person.
An *egalitarian* advocates *egalitarianism*.

cards.definition: selfish; believing that one is the center of everything
cards.example:
Nevitt was so *egocentric* that he could never give anyone else credit for doing anything.
*Egocentric* Lou never read the newspaper unless there was something in it about him.
It never occurred to the *egocentric* musician that his audiences might like to hear someone else’s songs every once in a while.
An *egoist* is an *egocentric* person. He believes the entire universe exists for his benefit.
cards.notes: An *egotist* is another type of *egocentric*. An *egotist* is an *egoist* who tells everyone how wonderful he is.

cards.definition: extremely bad; flagrant
cards.example:
The mother’s *egregious* neglect was responsible for her child’s accidental cross-country ride on the freight train.
Erik’s manners were *egregious;* he ate his mashed potatoes with his fingers and slurped the peas right off his plate.
cards.notes: Save this word for things that are worse than bad.

cards.definition: to bring out; to call forth
cards.example:
The interviewer skillfully *elicited* our true feelings by asking us questions that got to the heart of the matter.
The defendant tried to *elicit* the sympathy of the jury by appearing at the trial in a wheelchair, but the jury convicted him anyway.

cards.definition: oval; missing a word or words; obscure
cards.example:
The orbit of the earth is not perfectly round; it is *elliptical*.
The announcement from the State Department was purposely *elliptical*—the government didn’t really want reporters to know what was going on.
cards.notes:
This word has several meanings. Consult a dictionary if you are uncertain.
An egg may have an *elliptical* shape.
An *elliptical* statement is one that is hard or impossible to understand, either because something is missing from it or because the speaker or writer is trying to be hard to understand.

cards.definition: hard to pin down; evasive
cards.example:
The answer to the problem was *elusive;* every time the mathematician thought he was close, he discovered another error. (Or, one could say that the answer to the problem *eluded* the mathematician.)
The *elusive* criminal was next to impossible for the police to catch. (The criminal *eluded* the police.)
The team played hard, but victory was *elusive* and they suffered another defeat. (Victory *eluded* the hard-playing team.)
cards.notes: To be *elusive* is to *elude*, which means to avoid, evade, or escape.

cards.definition: to leave a country permanently; to expatriate
cards.example:
Pierre *emigrated* from France because he had grown tired of speaking French. Pierre became an *émigré* (EM uh gray).
The Soviet dissidents were persecuted by the secret police, so they sought permission to *emigrate*.
When Solange *emigrated* from France, she *immigrated* to the United States.
cards.notes:
= move from a country
At the heart of this word is the word *migrate*, which means to move from one place or country to another. *Emigrate* adds to migrate the sense of moving *out of* some place in particular.
On the other end of every *emigration* is an *immigration* (think of this as “in-migration”). See *immigration*.

cards.definition: well-known and respected; standing out from all others in quality or accomplishment; outstanding
cards.example:
The visiting poet was so *eminent* that our English teacher asked the poet for his autograph. Our English teacher thought the poet was *preeminent* in his field.
The entire audience fell silent when the *eminent* musician walked onto the stage and picked up his banjo and bongo drums.

cards.definition: relying on experience or observation; not merely theoretical
cards.example:
The apple-dropping experiment gave the scientists *empirical* evidence that gravity exists.
Nicky’s idea about the moon being made of pizza dough was not *empirical*.
We proved the pie’s deliciousness *empirically*, by eating it.

cards.definition: to strive to equal or excel, usually through imitation
cards.example:
To *emulate* someone is to try to be just as good as, or better than, him or her.
The American company *emulated* its successful Japanese competitor but never quite managed to do as well.
Little Joey imitated his athletic older brother in the hope of one day *emulating* his success.
I got ahead by *emulating* those who had succeeded before me.

cards.definition: to make gradual or stealthy inroads into; to trespass
cards.example:
As the city grew, it *encroached* on the countryside surrounding it.
With an *encroaching* sense of dread, I slowly pushed open the blood-spattered door.
My neighbor *encroached* on my yard by building his new stockade fence a few feet on my side of the property line.

cards.definition: native; restricted to a particular region or era; indigenous
cards.example:
You won’t find that kind of tree in California; it’s *endemic* to our part of the country.
That peculiar strain of influenza was *endemic* to a small community in South Carolina; there were no cases anywhere else.
The writer Tom Wolfe coined the term “Me Decade” to describe the egocentricity *endemic* in the 1970s.

cards.definition: to reduce the strength or energy of, especially to do so gradually
cards.example:
Sander felt *enervated* by his long ordeal and couldn’t make himself get out of bed.
Clinging to a flagpole for a month without food or water *enervated* me, and one day I fell asleep and ended up on the ground.
Life itself seemed to *enervate* the old man. He grew weaker and paler with every breath he drew.

cards.definition: to grant the privileges of citizenship, especially the right to vote
cards.example:
In the United States, citizens become *enfranchised* on their eighteenth birthdays. American women were not *enfranchised* until the adoption of the Nineteenth Amendment in 1920, which gave them the right to vote.
One of the goals of the reform candidate was to *disfranchise* the bodies at the cemetery, which had somehow managed to vote for the crooked mayor.
cards.notes:
= grant voting rights
To *disfranchise* (or *disenfranchise*) someone is to take away the privileges of citizenship or to take away the right to vote.

cards.definition: to bring into existence; to create; to cause
cards.example:
My winning lottery ticket *engendered* a great deal of envy among my co-workers; they all wished that they had won.
Smiles *engender* smiles.
The bitter lieutenant *engendered* discontent among his troops.

cards.definition: a mystery
cards.example:
Ben is an *enigma;* he never does any homework but he always gets good grades.
The wizard spoke in riddles and *enigmas*, and no one could understand what he was saying.
Ben’s good grades were *enigmatic*. So was the wizard’s speech.

cards.definition: extreme evil; a hideous offense; immensity
cards.example: Hitler’s soldiers stormed through the village, committing one *enormity* after another.
cards.notes: “Hugeness” or “great size” is not the main meaning of *enormity*. When you want to talk about the gigantic size of something, use *immensity* instead.

cards.definition: lasting a very short time
cards.example: The tread on those used tires will probably turn out to be *ephemeral*.
cards.notes:
*Ephemeral* comes from the Greek and means lasting a single day. The word is usually used more loosely to mean lasting a short time.
Youth and flowers are both *ephemeral*. They’re gone before you know it.
Some friendships are *ephemeral*.

cards.definition: a brief and usually witty or satirical saying
cards.notes:
= brief, witty saying
People often find it difficult to remember the difference between an *epigram* and an:
An *epigram* is *epigrammatic* (ep uh gruh MAT ik).

cards.definition: a brief summary that captures the meaning of the whole; the perfect example of something; a paradigm
cards.example:
The first paragraph of the new novel is an *epitome* of the entire book; you can read it and understand what the author is trying to get across. It *epitomizes* the entire work.
Luke’s freshman year was the *epitome* of a college experience; he made friends, joined a fraternity, and ate too much pizza.
Eating corn dogs and drinking root beer is the *epitome* of the good life, as far as Wilson is concerned.

cards.definition: composure; calm
cards.example:
The entire apartment building was crumbling, but Rachel faced the disaster with *equanimity*. She ducked out of the way of a falling beam and continued searching for an exit.
John’s mother looked at the broken glass on the floor with *equanimity;* at least he didn’t hurt himself when he knocked over the vase.

cards.definition: fair
cards.example:
King Solomon’s decision was certainly *equitable;* each mother would receive half the child.
The pirates distributed the loot *equitably* among themselves, so that each pirate received the same share as every other pirate.
The divorce settlement was quite *equitable*. Sheila got the right half of the house, and Tom got the left half.
cards.notes: *Equity* is fairness; *inequity* is unfairness. *Iniquity* and *inequity* both mean unfair, but *iniquity* implies wickedness as well. By the way, *equity* has a meaning in business. See our Finance chapter at the end of the book.

cards.definition: ambiguous; intentionally confusing; capable of being interpreted in more than one way
cards.example:
Joe’s response was *equivocal;* we couldn’t tell whether he meant yes or no, which is precisely what Joe wanted.
Dr. Festen’s *equivocal* diagnosis made us think that he had no idea what Mrs. Johnson had.
When we asked Harold whether that was his car that was parked in the middle of the hardware store, he *equivocated* and asked, “In which aisle?”
cards.notes:
*Ambiguous* means unclear. To be *equivocal* is to be intentionally ambiguous.
To be *equivocal* is to *equivocate*. To *equivocate* is to mislead by saying confusing or ambiguous things.

cards.definition: scholarly; deeply learned
cards.example:
The professor said such *erudite* things that none of us had the slightest idea of what he was saying.
The *erudite* biologist was viewed by many of his colleagues as a likely winner of the Nobel Prize.
Mr. Fernicola’s vast library was an indication of his *erudition*.
cards.notes: To be *erudite* is to possess *erudition* (er yoo DISH un), or extensive knowledge.

cards.definition: hard to understand; understood by only a select few; peculiar
cards.example:
Chicken wrestling and underwater yodeling were just two of Earl’s *esoteric* hobbies.
The author’s books were so *esoteric* that even his mother didn’t buy any of them.

cards.definition: to support; to advocate
cards.example:
The Mormons used to *espouse* bigamy, or marriage to more than one woman.
Alex *espoused* so many causes that he sometimes had trouble remembering which side he was on.
The candidate for governor *espoused* a program in which all taxes would be abolished and all the state’s revenues would be supplied by income from bingo and horse racing.

cards.definition: heavenly; as light and insubstantial as a gas or ether
cards.example:
The *ethereal* music we heard turned out to be not angels plucking on their harps but the wind blowing through the slats of the metal awning.
The *ethereal* mist on the hillside was delicate and beautiful.

cards.definition: a pleasant or inoffensive expression used in place of an unpleasant or offensive one
cards.example:
Aunt Angie, who couldn’t bring herself to say the word *death*, said that Uncle George had taken the big bus uptown. “Taking the big bus uptown” was her *euphemism* for dying.
The sex-education instructor wasn’t very effective. She was so embarrassed by the subject that she could only bring herself to speak *euphemistically* about it.

cards.definition: fleeting; vanishing; happening for only the briefest period
cards.example: Meteors are *evanescent:* They last so briefly that it is hard to tell whether one has actually appeared.

cards.definition: to make worse
cards.example:
Dipping Austin in lye *exacerbated* his skin condition.
The widow’s grief was *exacerbated* by the minister’s momentary inability to remember her dead husband’s name.
The fender-bender was *exacerbated* when two more cars plowed into the back of Margaret’s car.

cards.definition: extremely demanding; difficult; requiring great skill or care
cards.example:
The *exacting* math teacher subtracted points if you didn’t show every step of your work.
The surgeon’s *exacting* task was to reconnect the patient’s severed eyelid.

cards.definition: to raise high; to glorify
cards.example:
The manager decided to *exalt* the lowly batboy by asking him to throw the first pitch in the opening game of the World Series.
Diamante felt *exalted* when he woke up to discover that his great-uncle had left him $100 million.
Cleaning out a septic tank is not an *exalted* task.
cards.notes:
The adjective *exalted* is used frequently. Being queen of England is an *exalted* occupation.
Be careful not to confuse this word with *exult*, listed later.

cards.definition: to annoy thoroughly; to make very angry; to try the patience of
cards.example:
The child’s insistence on hopping backward on one foot *exasperated* his mother, who was in a hurry.
The algebra class’s refusal to answer any questions was extremely *exasperating* to the substitute teacher.

cards.definition: to illustrate by example; to serve as a good example
cards.example: Fred participated in every class discussion and typed all of his papers. His teacher thought Fred *exemplified* the model student; Fred’s classmates thought he was sycophantic.
cards.notes: An *exemplar* (ig ZEM plahr) is an ideal model or a paradigm. *Exemplary* (ig ZEM plur ee) means outstanding or worthy of imitation.

cards.definition: thorough; rigorous; complete; painstaking
cards.example: Before you use a parachute, you should examine it *exhaustively* for defects. Once you jump, your decision is irrevocable.

cards.definition: to urge strongly; to give a serious warning to
cards.example:
The coach used his bullhorn to *exhort* us to try harder.
The fearful forest ranger *exhorted* us not to go into the cave, but we did so anyway and became lost in the center of the earth.
cards.notes: The adjective is *hortatory* (HOR tuh tor ee).

cards.definition: an emergency; an urgency
cards.example: An academic *exigency:* You haven’t opened a book all term and the final is tomorrow morning.

cards.definition: having to do with existence; having to do with the body of thought called existentialism, which basically holds that human beings are responsible for their own actions but is otherwise too complicated to summarize in a single sentence
cards.notes: This word is overused but under-understood by virtually all of the people who use it. Unless you have a very good reason for throwing it around, you should probably avoid it.

cards.definition: to free completely from blame; to exculpate
cards.example:
The defendant, who had always claimed he wasn’t guilty, expected to be *exonerated* by the testimony of his best friend.
Our dog was *exonerated* when we discovered that it was in fact the cat that had eaten all the doughnuts.

cards.definition: to throw (someone) out of his or her native land; to move away from one’s native land; to emigrate
cards.example:
The rebels were *expatriated* by the nervous general, who feared that they would cause trouble if they were allowed to remain in the country.
Hugo was fed up with his native country, so he *expatriated* to America. In doing so, Hugo became an *expatriate* (eks PAY tree ut).
cards.notes:
= throw out of native land
To *repatriate* (ree PAY tree ayt) is to return to one’s native citizenship; that is, to become a *repatriate* (ree PAY tree it).

cards.definition: providing an immediate advantage; serving one’s immediate self-interest; practical
cards.example:
Since the basement had nearly filled with water, the plumber felt it would be *expedient* to clear out the drain.
The candidate’s position in favor of higher pay for teachers was an *expedient* one adopted for the national teachers’ convention but abandoned shortly afterward.
The car repairman did not have his tool kit handy, so he used chewing gum as an *expedient* to patch a hole.
cards.notes:
= immediately advantageous
*Expedient* can also be used as a noun for something *expedient*.
The noun *expedience* or *expediency* is practicality or being especially suited to a particular goal.

cards.definition: to speed up or ease the progress of
cards.example:
The post office *expedited* mail delivery by hiring more letter carriers.
The lawyer *expedited* the progress of our case through the courts by bribing a few judges.
Our wait for a table was *expedited* by a waiter who mistook Angela for a movie star.

cards.definition: clearly and directly expressed
cards.example:
The sexually *explicit* movie received an X rating.
The machine’s instructions were *explicit*—they told us exactly what to do.
No one *explicitly* asked us to set the barn on fire, but we got the impression that that was what we were supposed to do.
Gerry’s dissatisfaction with our work was *implicit* in his expression, although he never criticized us directly.
cards.notes:
= clearly expressed
*Implicit* means indirectly expressed or implied.

cards.definition: to praise highly; to laud
cards.example: The millionaire *extolled* the citizen who returned his gold watch but the only reward was a heartfelt handshake.

cards.definition: unnecessary; irrelevant; extra
cards.example:
Extra ice cream would never be *extraneous*, unless everyone had already eaten so much that no one wanted any more.
The book’s feeble plot was buried in a lot of *extraneous* material about a talking dog.
The salad contained several *extraneous* ingredients, including hair, sand, and a single dead fly.
cards.notes: To be *extraneous* is to be *extra* and always with the sense of being unnecessary.

cards.definition: to project or deduce from something known; to infer
cards.example:
George’s estimates were *extrapolated* from last year’s data; he simply took all the old numbers and doubled them.
Emeril came up with a probable recipe by *extrapolating* from the taste of the cookies he had eaten at the store.
By *extrapolating* from a handful of pottery fragments, the archaeologists formed a possible picture of the ancient civilization.
cards.notes: To *extrapolate*, a scientist uses the facts he has to project to facts outside; to *interpolate* (in TUR puh layt), he tries to fill the gaps within his data.

cards.definition: to free from difficulty
cards.example:
It took two and a half days to *extricate* the little girl from the abandoned well into which she had fallen.
Yoshi had to pretend to be sick to *extricate* himself from the blind date with the ventriloquist who brought her puppet on the date with her.
Monica had no trouble driving her car into the ditch, but she needed a tow truck to *extricate* it.
cards.notes: Something that is permanently stuck is *inextricable* (in EKS tri kuh bul).

cards.definition: an open, outgoing person; a person whose attention is focused on others rather than on himself or herself
cards.example:
Maria was quite an *extrovert;* she walked boldly into the roomful of strange adults and struck up many friendly conversations.
Damian was an *extrovert* in the sense that he was always more interested in other people’s business than in his own.
Ryan was an *introvert;* he spent virtually all his time in his room, writing in his diary and talking to himself. An *introvert* is usually introspective.
cards.notes: An *introvert* (IN truh vurt) is a person whose attention is directed inward and who is concerned with little outside himself or herself.

cards.definition: to rejoice; to celebrate
cards.example: The women’s team *exulted* in its victory over the men’s team at the badminton finals. They were *exultant*.

cards.definition: a lie; something made up
cards.example:
My story about being the prince of Wales was a *fabrication*. I’m really the king of Denmark.
The suspected murderer’s alibi turned out to be an elaborate *fabrication;* in other words, he was lying when he said that he hadn’t killed the victim.

cards.definition: humorous; not serious; clumsily humorous
cards.example:
David was sent to the principal’s office for making a *facetious* remark about the intelligence of the French teacher.
Our proposal about shipping our town’s garbage to the moon was *facetious*, but the first selectman took it seriously.

cards.definition: fluent; skillful in a superficial way; easy
cards.example:
Paolo’s poems were *facile* rather than truly accomplished; if you read them closely, you soon realized they were filled with clichés.
The CEO of the company was a *facile* speaker. He could speak engagingly on almost any topic with very little preparation. He spoke with great *facility*.
cards.notes:
= superficially skillful
To say that a writer’s style is *facile* is to say both that it is skillful and that it would be better if the writer exerted himself or herself more. The word *facile* almost always contains this sense of superficiality.

cards.definition: a group, usually a small part of a larger group, united around some cause; disagreement within an organization
cards.example:
At the Republican National Convention, the candidate’s *faction* spent much of its time shouting at the other candidate’s *faction*.
The faculty was relatively happy, but there was a *faction* that called for higher pay.
When the controversial topic of the fund drive came up, the committee descended into bitterness and *faction*. It was a *factious* topic.

cards.definition: absurd; ludicrous
cards.example:
The serious play quickly turned *farcical* when the leading man’s belt broke and his pants fell to his ankles.
The formerly secret documents detailed the CIA’s *farcical* attempt to discredit the dictator by sprinkling his shoes with a powder that was supposed to make his beard fall out.
cards.notes: *Farcical* means like a *farce*, which is a mockery or a ridiculous satire.

cards.definition: meticulous; demanding; finicky
cards.example:
Mrs. O’Hara was a *fastidious* housekeeper; she cleaned up our crumbs almost before they hit the floor.
Jeb was so *fastidious* in his work habits that he needed neither a wastebasket nor an eraser.
The *fastidious* secretary was nearly driven mad by her boss, who used the floor as a file cabinet and his desk as a pantry.

cards.definition: someone who believes that future events are already determined and that humans are powerless to change them
cards.example:
The old man was a *fatalist* about his illness, believing there was no sense in worrying about something he could not control.
Carmine was such a *fatalist* that he never wore a seat belt; he said that if he were meant to die in a car accident, there was nothing he could do to prevent it.
cards.notes:
= one who believes in fate
*Fatalist* is closely related to the word *fate*. A *fatalist* is someone who believes that *fate* determines everything.
To be a *fatalist* is to be *fatalistic*.

cards.definition: foolish; silly; idiotic
cards.example: Pauline is so pretty that her suitors are often driven to *fatuous* acts of devotion. They are *infatuated* with her.

cards.definition: animals
cards.example:
We saw little evidence of *fauna* on our walk through the woods. We did, however, see plenty of *flora*, or plants.
In Jim’s yard, the *flora* consists mostly of weeds.
cards.notes:
The phrase *flora* and *fauna* means plants and animals. The terms are used particularly in describing what lives in a particular region or environment.
Arctic *fauna* are very different from tropical *fauna*.
It’s easy to remember which of these words means what. Just replace *flora* and *fauna* with *flowers* and *fawns*.

cards.definition: fertile; productive
cards.example:
The *fecund* mother rabbit gave birth to hundreds and hundreds of little rabbits.
The child’s imagination was so *fecund* that dozens of stories hopped out of him like a bunch of baby rabbits.
Our compost heap became increasingly *fecund* as it decomposed.
cards.notes:
The state of being *fecund* is *fecundity* (fi KUN di tee).
This word can also be pronounced “FEK und.”

cards.definition: happiness; skillfulness, especially at expressing things; adeptness
cards.example:
Love was not all *felicity* for Judy and Steve; they argued all the time. In fact their relationship was characterized by *infelicity*.
Shakespeare wrote with great *felicity*. His works are filled with *felicitous* expressions.

cards.definition: great warmth or earnestness; ardor; zeal
cards.example: Avid baseball fans frequently display their *fervor* for the game by throwing food at bad players.

cards.definition: to restrain; to hamper
cards.example:
In his pursuit of an Olympic gold medal, the runner was *fettered* by multiple injuries.
After the dictator was deposed, a novelist produced a fictional account of the dictatorship that was *unfettered* by the strict rules of censorship.
The housewife’s young children were the *fetters* that prevented her from pursuing a second Master’s degree.
cards.notes:
To be *unfettered* is to be unrestrained or free of hindrances.
A *fetter* is literally a chain (attached to the foot) that is used to restrain a criminal or, for that matter, an innocent person. A figurative *fetter* can be anything that hampers or restrains someone.

cards.definition: faithfulness; loyalty
cards.example:
The motto of the United States Marine Corps is *semper fidelis*, which is Latin for always loyal.
The crusader’s life was marked by *fidelity* to the cause of justice.
The soldiers couldn’t shoot straight, but their *fidelity* to the cause of freedom was never in question.
cards.notes:
A *high-fidelity* record player is one that is very faithful in reproducing the original sound of whatever was recorded.
*Infidelity* means faithlessness or disloyalty. Marital *infidelity* is another way of saying adultery. Early phonograph records were marked by *infidelity* to the original.

cards.definition: based on figures of speech; expressing something in terms usually used for something else; metaphorical
cards.example:
When the mayor said that the housing market had sprouted wings, he was speaking *figuratively*. The housing market hadn’t really sprouted wings; it had merely risen so rapidly that it had almost seemed to fly.
Desmond could *literally* eat money if he chewed up and swallowed a dollar bill. Desmond’s car eats money only *figuratively*, in the sense that it is very expensive to operate.
cards.notes:
To say that the autumn hillside was a blaze of color is to use the word *blaze* in a *figurative* sense. The hillside wasn’t really on fire, but the colors of the leaves made it appear (somewhat) as though it were.
A *figurative* meaning of a word is one that is not *literal*. A *literal* statement is one in which every word means exactly what it says. If the housing market had *literally* sprouted wings, genuine wings would somehow have popped out of it.
People very, very often confuse these words, using one when they really mean the other.

cards.definition: skillful maneuvering; subtlety; craftiness
cards.example:
The doctor sewed up the wound with *finesse*, making stitches so small one could scarcely see them.
The boxer moved with such *finesse* that his opponent never knew what hit him.

cards.definition: glaringly bad; notorious; scandalous
cards.notes: An example of a *flagrant* theft would be stealing a car from the parking lot of a police station. A *flagrant* spelling error is a very noticeable one. See the listing for *blatant*, as these two words are often confused.

cards.definition: to show off; to display ostentatiously
cards.example:
The brand-new millionaire annoyed all his friends by driving around his old neighborhood to *flaunt* his new Rolls-Royce.
Colleen *flaunted* her engagement ring, shoving it in the face of almost anyone who came near her.
cards.notes: This word is very often confused with *flout*.

cards.definition: to disregard something out of disrespect
cards.example: A driver *flouts* the traffic laws by driving through red lights and knocking down pedestrians.
cards.notes:
= to disregard completely
To *flaunt* success is to make certain everyone knows that you are successful. To *flout* success is to be contemptuous of success or to act as though it means nothing at all.

cards.definition: a minor character flaw
cards.example:
Patti’s *foibles* included a tendency to prefer dogs to people.
The delegates to the state convention ignored the candidates’ positions on the major issues and concentrated on their *foibles*.

cards.definition: to stir up; to instigate
cards.example:
The bad news from abroad *fomented* pessimism among professional investors.
The radicals spread several rumors in an effort to *foment* rebellion among the peasants.

cards.definition: to refrain from; to abstain
cards.example:
Stephen told me I could become a millionaire if I joined him in his business, but his lack of integrity makes me nervous so I decided to *forbear*.
George *forbore* to punch me in the nose, even though I told him that I thought he was a sniveling idiot.
cards.notes:
The noun is *forbearance*.
A *forebear* (FOR bayr)—sometimes also spelled *forbear*—is an ancestor.

cards.definition: to do without; to forbear
cards.example: We had some of the chocolate cake, some of the chocolate mousse, and some of the chocolate cream pie, but we were worried about our weight so we decided to *forego* the chocolate-covered potato chips. That is, we *forewent* them.

cards.definition: to abandon; to renounce; to relinquish
cards.example:
We urged Buddy to *forsake* his life with the alien beings and return to his job at the drugstore.
All the guru’s followers had *forsaken* him, so he became a real estate developer and turned his temple into an apartment building.

cards.definition: accidental; occurring by chance
cards.example:
The program’s outcome was not the result of any plan but was entirely *fortuitous*.
The object was so perfectly formed that its creation could not have been *fortuitous*.
cards.notes: *Fortuitous* is often misused to mean lucky or serendipitous. Don’t make that same mistake. It means merely accidental.

cards.definition: to fail; to collapse; to sink
cards.example:
The candidate’s campaign for the presidency *foundered* when it was revealed that he had once been married to a drug addict.
Zeke successfully struggled through the first part of the course but *foundered* when the final examination was given.
The ship *foundered* shortly after it hit the iceberg.
Our field hockey team *floundered* helplessly around the field while the opposing team scored goal after goal.
The witness began to *flounder* as the attorney fired question after question.
cards.notes:
Be careful not to confuse this word with *flounder*, which means to move clumsily or in confusion.
If you want to remember the difference between the two words, think that when a person *flounders*, he is flopping around like a flounder.

cards.definition: like brothers
cards.example:
The *fraternal* feelings of the group were strengthened by monthly fishing trips.
A *fraternity* is an organization of men who have bound themselves together in a relationship analogous to that of real brothers.

cards.definition: frantic; frenzied
cards.example:
There was a lot of *frenetic* activity in the office, but nothing ever seemed to get accomplished.
The bird’s *frenetic* attempt to free itself from the thorn bush only made the situation worse.

cards.definition: economical; penny-pinching
cards.example:
Laura was so *frugal* that she even tried to bargain with the checkout girl at the discount store.
We were as *frugal* as we could be, but we still ended up several thousand dollars in debt.
Hannah’s *frugality* annoyed her husband, who loved spending money on tech gadgets.

cards.definition: secretive; sly
cards.example:
Cal wiggled his ears while the countess was talking to him in a *furtive* attempt to catch our attention.
The burglars were *furtive*, but not *furtive* enough; the alert policeman grabbed them as they carried the TV through the Rubenstein’s back door.

cards.definition: useless; hopeless
cards.example:
A D+ average and no extracurricular interests to speak of meant that applying to Harvard was *futile*, but Lucinda hoped against hope.
Lucinda doesn’t know what a *futility* it is.
cards.notes: Something *futile* is a *futility* (fyoo TIL uh tee).

cards.definition: talkative; chatty
cards.example: Gabriella is gregarious and *garrulous;* she loves to hang out with the gang and gab.

cards.definition: unskillful; awkward; maladroit
cards.example: Smadar had a poor sense of comic timing, and her *gauche* attempts to mock her left-handed friends soon left her with none.
cards.notes:
= socially awkward
Remember *dextrous*? Well, *gauche* is pretty much the exact opposite. It is the French word for left—the connection is that left-handed people were once thought to be clumsy (this was clearly before the invention of left-handed scissors) and perverse, even evil. These days, *gauche* tends to describe social, rather than physical, ineptness.

cards.definition: a type or category, especially of art or writing
cards.example: Daoyen displayed a great talent for a particular *genre:* the bawdy limerick.
cards.notes:
= type of art
The novel is one literary *genre*. Poetry is another.

cards.definition: refined; polite; aristocratic; affecting refinement
cards.example: The ladies at the ball were too *genteel* to accept our invitation to the wrestling match.

cards.definition: to make gestures, especially when speaking or in place of speaking
cards.example:
Massimo *gesticulated* wildly on the other side of the theater in an attempt to get our attention.
The after-dinner speaker *gesticulated* in such a strange way that the audience paid more attention to his hands than to his words.

cards.definition: surplus; an overabundance
cards.example:
